papers.title: Frequency-Adaptive Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Text-to-Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Flow matching (FM) enables efficient acoustic modeling for text-to-speech (TTS), but fine spectral structures may remain imperfectly reconstructed. To address this issue, we propose frequency-adaptive flow matching (FAFM), which replaces the shared linear interpolation schedule with a frequency-dependent nonlinear schedule. By assigning different interpolation exponents to Mel-frequency bands, FAFM advances high-frequency components earlier along their conditional paths while preserving the endpoints of the linear baseline. The corresponding analytical target velocity modulates frequency-dependent evolution without introducing additional network modules. Evaluations across two TTS architectures and English and Chinese datasets show improvements in spectral reconstruction and several objective quality and intelligibility metrics. Results averaged over three independent training seeds, together with band-wise spectral analysis, support the effectiveness of moderate frequency modulation. Subjective listening tests show small numerical gains in perceived naturalness over standard CFM.

papers.title: BinauralLM: spatial prompted text-to-binaural audio generation with large language model
papers.abstract: Binaural audio is a practical spatial audio format for headphone playback and is widely used in immersive media such as games, VR/AR, and interactive multimedia. Currently, binaural audio is still largely obtained either by specialized recordings or by spatializing pre-recorded monaural signals, which limits flexibility for controllable content creation. While recent text-to-audio models can generate the required audio, most of them target monaural output or unconstrained stereo. They provide limited control over spatial attributes such as direction and motion. To address these challenges, we propose BinauralLM, a spatial prompted text-to-binaural audio generation framework with large language model (LLM). BinauralLM adopts a two-stage pipeline. First, we use a Qwen2.5 LLM to autoregressively generate coarse binaural token sequences conditioned on text and spatial prompts. To effectively couple semantic content with spatial cues, we introduce a spatial prompt encoder and an attention fusion module to produce a unified conditioning representation for binaural token generation. Second, we employ a flow matching model that takes the coarse binaural tokens as conditions and reconstructs high-quality binaural waveforms in the continuous domain. Experimental results on the BEWO-1M dataset demonstrate that BinauralLM achieves superior performance on standard text-to-audio metrics and binaural spatial metrics, and achieves higher MOS scores in perceptual evaluation, especially on spatialization quality. These results indicate that our proposed method offers an effective route to controllable and high-quality text-to-binaural audio generation.
papers.venue: Journal on Audio, Speech, and Music Processing
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: audio generation, text-to-audio

Website · GitHub · The guide · ☕ Buy me a Coffee Machine

> Ruach Studio is open music generation that runs on your own hardware: the model, the score, the adapters and every take stay yours, and nothing is rented by the token. Open models are now good enough to stand on their own, and what was missing is the studio around them: that is what we build, in the open. Music should be free to make and to share: whoever has no voice, no instrument and no studio still has the right to lay their thoughts and feelings onto sound. > **⚠ Not on free cloud GPUs.** Ruach Studio does not run on Google Colab, Kaggle or any free notebook GPU, so don't spend an evening on it there: it is a whole studio, not a notebook. It builds its C++/CUDA engine on the machine it lives on, keeps a server and a lab of Python services running beside it, and takes about 33 GB of disk (60 GB with the Artist). A free session's card, memory, wiped disk and hours-long limit cannot hold that. It wants your own Linux computer, or a server you rent and keep, with an NVIDIA card: 24 GB for everything, 16 GB with the smaller model copies. Everything [Ruach Studio](https://github.com/igrbible/Ruach_Studio) runs on, in one place and laid out as its own folders: the music model and its decoders, the transcriber, the stems' and the sound upscaler's models, Whisper, the style listener, the studio's own adapters, the LoRA Trainer's base, and the Artist's painters with the adapters their authors let be shared. 1662 files, 501 GB. A copy of the studio's own disk, file for file: what lies here is what it paints, sings and trains with, and the studio fetches all of it from here alone. **Nothing here is ours but the conversions and the studio's own adapters.** Every other file is its authors' work, unchanged, under its authors' licence, credited below and line by line in `MANIFEST.tsv`. Not affiliated with M-A-P, Comfy Org, Mothersuperior, HaileyStorm, atomtanstudio, storagejuju, OpenAI, Systran, Meta, the Qwen team, Unsloth, lightx2v, Falconsai, prithivMLmods, Civitai or the authors named below. If you are an author and want a file of yours taken down, open a discussion here and it goes. ## Take what you need The studio's own install (`./fetch-models.sh`) takes what your card can run, at a pinned revision, checking each file. By hand, from the studio's root: ```bash hf download goldhub/Ruach_Studio_Models_v2 --local-dir . --include "models/YuE2-3B-Q8_0.gguf" "models/YuE2-Vae-F32.gguf" "models/SheetSage2-Q8_0.gguf" "models/MERT-v2-FullSong-Q8_0.gguf" # to sing: 5.3 GB hf download goldhub/Ruach_Studio_Models_v2 --local-dir . --include "models/YuE2-Vae-*" # the other decoders hf download goldhub/Ruach_Studio_Models_v2 --local-dir . --include "models/SheetSage2-Refined-F16.gguf" "models/SheetSage2-Refined/*" # the second transcriber (beside SheetSage2): 0.16 GB hf download goldhub/Ruach_Studio_Models_v2 --local-dir . --include "whisper/*" "separation/*" "universr/*" # Whisper, stems, the sound's upscaler hf download goldhub/Ruach_Studio_Models_v2 --local-dir . --include "artwork/upscalers/*" "licenses/upscalers/*" # the Artist's upscalers hf download goldhub/Ruach_Studio_Models_v2 --local-dir . --include "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/gguf/*Q4_K_M*" "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/lightning/*" "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/*.json" "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/scheduler/*" "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/tokenizer/*" "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/text_encoder/*" "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/vae/*" "artwork/Qwen-Image-2512/transformer/*" # the Artist on 16 GB hf download goldhub/Ruach_Studio_Models_v2 --local-dir . --include "checkpoints/comfy/checkpoints/yue2_3b_bf16.safetensors" "checkpoints/MERT-v2-FullSong/*" "checkpoints/yue2-mothersuperior-realaudio-tokenizer-v4/*" # the LoRA Trainer's base: 10.5 GB ``` ## Known by its content, not its name `SHA256SUMS` holds each file's SHA-256 (as `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS` reads it, and as Hugging Face knows the file). `MANIFEST.tsv` adds, for each `.safetensors`, the SHA-256 of its tensors alone (their names and data, its header's metadata aside), with each file's origin and licence. # StaleyNET checkpoints

[![Source on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/source-GitHub-1D1B20?logo=github)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet) [![staleynet-audio on crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/staleynet-audio?label=staleynet-audio)](https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/paper-PDF-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/blob/main/paper/preprint.pdf) [![Book](https://img.shields.io/badge/book-mdBook-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/tree/main/book/src) [![Release v0.1.2](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/arpanpathak/staleynet)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases) [![Dataset: 3.1 GB](https://img.shields.io/badge/dataset-3.1%20GB-FFD21E?logo=huggingface&logoColor=black)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arpanpathak/staleynet-data)

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

## At a glance

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Checkpointed runs | 9 |
| Parameters | 7,099,904 for text-only runs; 7,165,440 for the lyrics runs; 42,858,496 for `pq-large` |
| Transformer | width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, context 768 (`pq-large`: width 512, 8 layers, context 1152) |
| Audio tokens | 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries (`pq-large`: 4 band groups × 4 levels = 16 codebooks of 1024 entries) |
| Audio features | 128 mel bands at 24 kHz, FFT 1024, hop 256 |
| Training data | Song Describer Dataset and JamendoLyrics MultiLang |
| License | CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream dataset terms |

## Checkpoints

| Run | Purpose | Parameters | `best` step | `latest` step | Training tracks |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `thor-base` | base text-to-music model | 7,099,904 | 0 | None | 667 |
| `smoke` | pipeline smoke test | 7,099,904 | 0 | 1,500 | 667 |
| `overfit-one-take` | single-take memorisation check | 7,099,904 | 200 | 200 | 1 |
| `vocal-scratch` | vocal-filtered model from scratch | 7,099,904 | 5,500 | 6,000 | 281 |
| `vocal-finetune` | vocal fine-tune | 7,099,904 | 250 | None | 281 |
| `lyrics-orin` | lyrics-conditioned model | 7,165,440 | 3,750 | 4,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor` | lyrics-conditioned model trained on the AGX Thor | 7,165,440 | 4,750 | 8,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor-long` | the same model trained for 20,000 steps | 7,165,440 | 19,750 | 20,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `pq-large` | larger model on the band-group tokenizer (in progress) | 42,858,496 | 7,000 | 7,000 | 742 (75 with lyrics) |

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

The checkpoint files are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0 (`LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt`) to the extent the upstream dataset licenses allow. See `NOTICE` for the full provenance statement and `SHA256SUMS` for integrity.

## Known limitations

- Griffin-Lim produces phasey audio compared with a learned vocoder.
- The models are small edge models, not production music systems.
- The lyric models were trained on a small lyrics subset, so lyric intelligibility is limited.
- The checkpoints are research artifacts and have no warranty.

# TuneJury — instance-level pairwise reward model for text-to-music

TuneJury is a 2.8M-parameter MLP head over frozen LAION-CLAP-Music + MERT-v1-330M
embeddings, trained with a shared-weight pairwise-logistic objective on ~17.5K human
A vs. B preferences from four open sources. It scores a single audio clip (with an
optional text prompt) as one preference scalar.

- **Paper:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17006
- **Project Page:** https://yonghyunk1m.github.io/TuneJury/
- **Code:** https://github.com/yonghyunk1m/TuneJury
- **Demo:** https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuneJury/tune-jury-demo
- **Scope:** trained and evaluated on instrumental music. For prompt formats unlike the
  live-arena style it was trained on (e.g. post-hoc captions), an empty prompt can be the
  safer default (paper §4.2). Anchor calibration adapts to newly released generators
  without retraining.

## Checkpoints

| File | Encoder / mix | License |
|---|---|---|
| `tunejury.pt` | CLAP+MERT, 4-dataset (primary) | CC-BY-NC 4.0 |
| `tunejury_muq_leave_MA.pt` | MuQ-MuLan-large encoder-swap | CC-BY-NC 4.0 |
| `A1_clap_audio_only.pt` | CLAP-audio-only | Apache-2.0 |
| `B1L_clap2_large_audio_only.pt` | CLAP2-Large audio-only, 4-dataset (new) | Apache-2.0 |
| `B1S_clap2_small_audio_only.pt` | CLAP2-Small audio-only, 4-dataset (new) | Apache-2.0 |
| `tunejury_leave_*.pt` | leave-one / leave-two-out (fair-eval) | CC-BY-NC 4.0 |

## Quick scoring

Install the package (also pulls the LAION-CLAP encoder ~2.2 GB on first use; needs
`ffmpeg` and `libsndfile`):

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/yonghyunk1m/TuneJury
```

```python
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from tunejury.score import Scorer

sc = Scorer.from_pretrained(hf_hub_download("TuneJury/tunejury", "tunejury.pt"))
print(sc.score("clip.wav", ""))   # "" -> 512-d zero text vector (paper §3/§4.2 empty-prompt)
print(sc.score("clip.wav", "a calm lo-fi piano loop"))   # a prompt uses the text branch
```

## CLAP2 audio-only heads (B1L, B1S)

Two additional heads over the frozen [LAION CLAP2](https://huggingface.co/laion/clap2-large-audioxl-s1B)
audio encoder (Large 340M, Small 104M). They use the primary head's MLP, training pairs,
objective and hyperparameters (seed 42). Only the input differs: one CLAP2 audio embedding,
with no MERT and no text. They add an audio-only option with an Apache-2.0 head and encoder.
The existing checkpoints are unchanged.

Same evaluation code for every row. "MA 2026-02/03" is the 799 decisive Feb–Mar 2026 Music
Arena battles, collected after the training cutoff.

| Checkpoint | Internal | MA 2026-02/03 | CMI MA | CMI-Pref | PAM SRCC | MusicEval SRCC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tunejury.pt`, with prompt | 0.7086 | 0.5369 | **0.7194** | 0.7220 | 0.5906 | 0.6441 |
| `tunejury.pt`, empty prompt | 0.7086 | 0.5307 | 0.7090 | 0.6980 | 0.6734 | 0.6441 |
| `A1_clap_audio_only.pt` | 0.7052 | **0.5557** | 0.6754 | 0.6800 | 0.5873 | 0.5747 |
| `B1L_clap2_large_audio_only.pt` | **0.7086** | 0.5532 | 0.6858 | **0.7500** | **0.7078** | **0.7326** |
| `B1S_clap2_small_audio_only.pt` | 0.6988 | 0.5307 | 0.6978 | 0.7140 | 0.6979 | 0.6944 |

Internal, MA and CMI-Pref columns report pairwise accuracy. Over three training seeds the CLAP2-L
audio-only configuration averages PAM 0.668 ± 0.034 and MusicEval 0.723 ± 0.010, versus
0.568 ± 0.017 and 0.552 ± 0.033 for LAION-CLAP audio-only. PAM and MusicEval values can differ by
up to about 0.03 from the official CMI-RewardBench harness, which applies its own clip-length cap.

Features must match training. Decode at the native sample rate (no 16 kHz step) and mix to mono.
Split the clip into non-overlapping 30 s windows from the start, at most four. Average the
L2-normalised CLAP2 window embeddings and re-normalise the mean. The standalone scorer does this:

```bash
pip install "open_clip_torch==4.2.2" soundfile huggingface_hub torchaudio
wget https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuneJury/tune-jury/resolve/main/clap2_only.py
python clap2_only.py clip.wav --size large     # or --size small
```

Details, checksums and preprocessing notes:
[CLAP2_ONLY.md](https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuneJury/tune-jury/blob/main/CLAP2_ONLY.md).
The heads are also selectable in the [interactive demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuneJury/tune-jury).

![BA: Your Voice. Your Identity.](https://huggingface.co/mahmoudalyosify/BA/resolve/main/assets/banner.png)

# BA · Your Voice. Your Identity.

BA speaks any text in your own voice, from a 10–15 second recording of you: **Egyptian Arabic**, **English**, and **French (beta)**. Every output carries an inaudible watermark. Use only your own voice or a voice whose owner has given you explicit permission.

**Try it:** [the BA Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mahmoudalyosify/BA) (record or upload your voice, tick the consent box, type, listen).

## What BA is, and what it is built from

BA v0.1.0 is two things:

1. **The VoxCPM2 weights, unmodified.** VoxCPM2 is a 2B-parameter, 48 kHz multilingual text-to-speech model by OpenBMB, released under Apache-2.0. The weight and tokenizer files in this repository are byte-for-byte copies of [`openbmb/VoxCPM2`](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2) at commit `7936080b41163874f38610f46f438e2c0757f9fd` (see `NOTICE`). BA v0.1 does **not** fine-tune or otherwise change them.
2. **The BA engine** (`ba_tts`, this repository's wheel), which decides how the model is driven:
   - prepares the reference recording (mono, trimmed to speech, loudness-normalised, the cleanest stretch chosen; noisy, clipped or too-short audio is refused with a clear message);
   - transcribes the reference with Whisper large-v3-turbo when you give no transcript, and clones with the reference *and* its transcript;
   - writes digits, times, prices, percentages and symbols as Egyptian, English or French words, and writes common English loanwords in Egyptian text in Arabic script;
   - splits long text at sentence boundaries, checks every chunk (duration against text length, empty or clipped audio) and regenerates failures with a new seed;
   - loudness-normalises the result and embeds an [AudioSeal](https://huggingface.co/facebook/audioseal) watermark.

VoxCPM2 was chosen in a bake-off of eight voice-cloning systems on Egyptian Arabic (below). Of the systems eligible as a base (permissively licensed weights with documented training data), it was the only one whose Egyptian output a dialect classifier labelled as Egyptian most of the time.

## Quick start

Python 3.10 or newer. A CUDA GPU is strongly recommended (peak GPU memory in our runs: 8.11 GB allocated, 10.99 GB reserved); CPU works but is slow.

```bash
pip install https://huggingface.co/mahmoudalyosify/BA/resolve/main/ba_tts-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
```

```python
import soundfile as sf
from ba_tts import BA, detect_watermark

ba = BA.from_pretrained("mahmoudalyosify/BA")      # downloads the weights (about 5 GB) on first use
voice = ba.create_voice("my_voice.wav", language="arz")   # 10-15 s of YOUR voice; transcript optional

sr, wav = ba.speak("الميعاد اتغير للساعة 7:30، والتذكرة بقت ب 150 جنيه.", voice, language="arz")
sf.write("out.wav", wav, sr)                        # 48 kHz, watermarked

print(detect_watermark(wav, sr))                    # {'watermarked': True, 'score': ..., 'bits_match': ...}
```

`language` is `"arz"` (Egyptian Arabic), `"en"` or `"fr"`. You can pass several recordings (`create_voice(["a.wav", "b.wav"])`), give the transcript yourself (`transcript="..."`), save a voice for later (`voice.save("me.npz")`, `Voice.load("me.npz")`), and set `seed`, `cfg_value` or `inference_timesteps` in `speak`. Text longer than one chunk is split and joined automatically (up to 5,000 characters).

Command line:

```bash
ba-tts --ref my_voice.wav --lang arz --text "أنا رايح الشغل دلوقتي وهرجع على المغرب." --out out.wav
ba-tts --ref my_voice.wav --lang en --text-file speech.txt --out speech.wav --save-voice me.npz
ba-tts --detect out.wav          # is this file a BA output?
```

## Languages

A language is listed only if the full system passes gate G3 on held-out texts: failure rate at most 5%; intelligibility within a fixed bound; speaker similarity at least 80% of the similarity between two real recordings of the same speaker; and, for Egyptian, a dialect-ID share at least 60% of the share measured on real colloquial Egyptian speech (otherwise it would be listed only as "Arabic").

Cross-language use (an Egyptian voice speaking English or French) works, with lower similarity (see Limitations).

## Measured results

### Evaluation set

- **Reference voices:** 12 speakers from [FLEURS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/fleurs) (CC-BY-4.0): 6 Egyptian (`ar_eg`, 3 male and 3 female), 3 American English, 3 French; clean clips of 8–15 s. They are used for measurement only; neither these clips nor anything cloned from them is published.
- **Texts:** 40 colloquial Egyptian sentences (everyday talk, questions, numbers and dates, long sentences, a diacritised copy of ten), 20 English, 20 French, 6 Arabic–English code-switched sentences, and one passage of about 120 words per language. Some texts were used to tune the engine; **every number below excludes them** (held-out texts only). BA and raw VoxCPM2 are compared on the same texts, voices and seeds.
- **Automatic metrics, each calibrated on real speech:**
  - words: CER (Egyptian) and WER (English, French) from Whisper large-v3 after normalisation. On real speech the same ASR gives CER 0.071 on colloquial Egyptian and WER 0.052 (English) and 0.062 (French) on FLEURS;
  - voice: cosine similarity of ECAPA-TDNN speaker embeddings between the reference and the output. Two different real clips of the same speaker score 0.870 (Egyptian), 0.874 (English), 0.900 (French); clips of different speakers 0.084–0.184;
  - dialect: share of outputs that the [`badrex/mms-300m-arabic-dialect-identifier`](https://huggingface.co/badrex/mms-300m-arabic-dialect-identifier) classifier labels Egyptian. colloquial Egyptian speech: 0.90 (lahgtna test set; the gate's reference) and 0.98 (NileTTS); Egyptians reading Modern Standard Arabic (FLEURS): 0.34;
  - naturalness: DNSMOS P.808 (real speech: 3.515–3.990);
  - failures: empty, cut off, or a duration far outside what the text length implies.

## How it works

```
your recording(s) ──► reference preparation ──► Whisper large-v3-turbo transcript (if none given)
                                 │                               │
                                 └──────► VoxCPM2 prompt cache (reference audio + transcript)
text ──► language normaliser (numbers, symbols, loanwords) ──► sentence chunks
                                                                 │
          VoxCPM2 generation per chunk, fixed voice and seed ◄───┘
                     │
          chunk check (duration vs text length, empty, clipped) ──► retry with a new seed (up to 2)
                     │
          join with pauses ──► loudness normalisation (−20 LUFS) ──► AudioSeal watermark ──► 48 kHz audio
```

The per-language generation settings (guidance 2.0, 10 steps), the chunk length, the reference noise thresholds and the loanword policy were chosen by measurement on the tuning texts. They are recorded in `ba_config.json`, which also pins the revisions of the ASR model and the watermark weights.

## Limitations

- **No native-listener review yet.** Nobody has yet listened systematically to BA's outputs; the owner's blind listening test of the bake-off is pending. Every quality number on this card is automatic.
- **Automatic metrics have blind spots.** One dialect classifier decides "Egyptian"; it labels Egyptians reading Modern Standard Arabic as Egyptian only 34% of the time, and the six Egyptian reference voices are FLEURS clips of read MSA, not colloquial speech. DNSMOS was trained on English and is a weak judge of Arabic. Similarity is one embedding model (ECAPA).
- **Digits are measured by ASR.** Whisper writes most spoken numbers back as digits, so the digit-sentence CER shows whether the right number was said, not whether it was said the Egyptian way. The normaliser itself is covered by unit tests.
- **Small sets.** 18 digit sentences, 18 code-switched utterances and 2 passages per language; French rests on 3 voices.
- **Cross-language similarity is lower.** An Egyptian voice speaking French reaches similarity 0.696, exactly 80% of the Egyptian same-speaker ceiling (0.870); speaking English, 0.730. Cross-language use was not part of the gate.
- **Code-switching.** Inside Egyptian text, a fixed list of common English loanwords is written in Arabic script and short upper-case acronyms are spelled letter by letter; other Latin words are left as written and may be mispronounced.
- **Speed.** Timings are on an A40. The Space runs on shared ZeroGPU hardware, where speed and queueing differ. CPU-only use is very slow.
- **Reference quality matters.** Noisy, reverberant, clipped or very short recordings are refused or give a weaker likeness.
- **No fine-tune.** BA v0.1 uses the base weights; anything VoxCPM2 cannot say well, BA cannot either.

## Responsible use

- **Consent.** Use only your own voice, or a voice whose owner has given you explicit permission for this use. Do not impersonate anyone, deceive, defraud, harass, or make non-consensual content. These terms are part of the licence.
- **Watermark.** Every BA output carries an inaudible AudioSeal watermark with the 16-bit message "BA". Anyone can check a file: `ba-tts --detect file.wav`, or `detect_watermark(wav, sr)` in Python. Detection survived MP3 at 64 kbit/s and resampling in our tests; it was not tested against deliberate removal attacks. Do not remove or circumvent it, and do not publish audio made with the watermark switched off (`watermark=False` exists for research measurement).
- **The Space.** Generation is blocked until you tick the consent box. Uploads are processed in a per-request temporary directory that is deleted after the request, together with Gradio's own copies; the voice prepared from them lives only in your browser session's memory. Generated audio sits in Gradio's cache only so the player and download work, and is swept every few minutes. No text or audio is logged; flagging and analytics are off. Nothing you upload is used for training.

# OGG TTS **Expressive multilingual text-to-speech with block diffusion**
> **Preview release.** This is checkpoint 430k of a pre-training run that ended at 440k steps, with a new > acoustic decoder (axial MTP). The earlier 20k and 40k previews (previous architecture) and the 120k preview stay > available in the history of this repository. ## Overview OGG TTS is a 0.75B-parameter zero-shot text-to-speech model trained on about 8,200 hours of studio-quality speech in English, Polish, Spanish, German, Russian, French, Portuguese and Italian. It generates discrete tokens of the Fish Audio 44.1 kHz codec with **block diffusion**: - each block of 0.74 s is produced in parallel by iterative unmasking; - blocks follow one another left to right, so audio can be streamed as soon as the first block is ready. The backbone is initialised from OmniVoice (Qwen3-0.6B, masked discrete diffusion). An axial multi-token prediction (MTP) decoder then fills in the acoustic detail of the block: the 9 residual codebooks, one per step, for all frames at once. The name comes from the trolls of *The Witcher*. OGG is the first of three architectures (OGG, ROGG, POGG) that we compare in an upcoming technical report. ### Highlights - **Expressive by default.** The model reads with natural, context-appropriate emotion. - **Optional inline tags.** 24 tags for emotion, delivery and vocal events, placed exactly where they should take effect. - **Zero-shot voice cloning.** From a few seconds of reference audio, or one of the built-in speaker identities without any prompt. - **Context-aware delivery.** Neighbouring lines can be given as text context, so a line of dialogue or a sentence of a story fits its scene. - **Streaming.** Finished blocks never change and can be played immediately. ## Emotion and expression tags Tags are optional. Without them the model infers the delivery from the text and its context. With them it follows the requested emotion or sound at the given position: ```text [frustrated] Not again… [sighing] Fine, I'll do it myself. [scared] [whispering] Someone is here… [shouting] Run! They're right behind us! ``` | Group | Tags | |---|---| | Emotion | `[angry]` `[frustrated]` `[excited]` `[tired]` `[playful]` `[sad]` `[scared]` `[shouting]` | | Delivery | `[whispering]` `[softly]` `[voice breaking]` `[singing]` `[pause]` `[slowly]` | | Vocal events | `[laughing]` `[sighing]` `[gasping]` `[panting]` `[coughing]` `[clears throat]` `[sniffling]` `[scoffing]` `[yawning]` `[humming]` | The labels come from an audio-language-model pass over **502,668 sentences**, i.e. the audio with its transcript, under a closed list of 24 tags. The model was instructed to tag only what is audible in the recording, never what the text alone suggests. 57,016 sentences (11 %) received at least one tag; the rest carry a checked transcript without tags, so the model also learns when *not* to add an effect. Tags are dropped from part of the training samples, which keeps them optional at inference time. | Tag | Examples | Tag | Examples | Tag | Examples | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `[shouting]` | 19,407 | `[laughing]` | 2,621 | `[tired]` | 708 | | `[angry]` | 10,287 | `[scared]` | 1,847 | `[slowly]` | 419 | | `[frustrated]` | 5,565 | `[whispering]` | 1,502 | `[clears throat]` | 356 | | `[pause]` | 4,065 | `[playful]` | 1,380 | `[humming]` | 346 | | `[excited]` | 3,980 | `[gasping]` | 1,266 | `[coughing]` | 333 | | `[sighing]` | 3,738 | `[scoffing]` | 1,010 | `[panting]` | 248 | | | | `[sad]` | 894 | `[voice breaking]` | 144 | | | | `[softly]` | 887 | `[singing]` | 95 | Rare tags (`[singing]`, `[yawning]` 59, `[sniffling]` 46) have too few examples to be reliable. Tag control is still weak in early checkpoints and strengthens as pre-training continues. ## Model architecture | Component | Details | |---|---| | Backbone | OmniVoice / Qwen3-0.6B, 28 layers, d = 1024. Bidirectional attention within a block, block-causal across blocks; earlier blocks are seen with all 10 codebooks | | Acoustic decoder | Axial MTP, 110M parameters: 6 layers over a (frame × codebook) grid, each with attention across the codebooks of a frame (causal) and across the frames of a codebook (the prompt, earlier blocks and the current block) | | Total parameters | ~0.75B (codec excluded) | | Audio codec | Fish Audio Drama 3 / S2 codec, 44.1 kHz, 21.5 frames/s, 1 semantic codebook (4096) + 9 residual codebooks (1024) | | Block size | 16 frames (0.74 s) | | Decoding | 6 confidence-ordered unmasking iterations per block with classifier-free guidance, then 9 axial-MTP steps (one per residual codebook); KV cache | | Length | predicted by the model (end-of-speech token) | ## Usage Requires the [code from GitHub](https://github.com/FashionFlora/ogg-tts), the OmniVoice weights (`k2-fsa/OmniVoice`) and the Fish Audio codec (`codec.pth` from `fishaudio/drama-3`). ```bash git clone https://github.com/FashionFlora/ogg-tts && cd ogg-tts git clone https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech ogg_tts/fish-speech export OMNIVOICE_PATH=$(huggingface-cli download k2-fsa/OmniVoice) export FISH_CODEC_PATH=$(huggingface-cli download fishaudio/drama-3 codec.pth) ``` ```python import sys sys.path.insert(0, "ogg_tts") from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download import infer_omnifish as inf, fish_codec as fc model, tok = inf.load_model(hf_hub_download("FashionFlora/ogg-tts", "model.safetensors"), "cuda") codec = fc.load_codec("cuda") codes = inf.generate_cached(model, tok, None, "", "[sighing] Hello! I am OGG, a text to speech model.", "en", cfg=1.5) audio = fc.decode(codec, codes[None].cuda())[0].float().cpu().numpy() # 44.1 kHz ``` **Voice cloning:** pass the reference audio's codes (`fc.encode`) and its exact transcript: ```python ref, _ = fc.encode(codec, wav_44k[None].cuda()) # wav_44k: torch tensor, mono, 44.1 kHz, up to ~15 s codes = inf.generate_cached(model, tok, ref[0].cpu(), "Transcript of the reference.", "Text to speak.", "en", cfg=1.5) ``` **Context:** neighbouring lines (not spoken) set the delivery, e.g. for a line of dialogue or the next sentence of a story: ```python codes = inf.generate_cached(model, tok, ref[0].cpu(), ref_text, "[frustrated] I told you already. I was at work.", "en", semantic_left=("Where were you last night?",), after=("At three in the morning?",), cfg=1.5) ``` **Guidance and pace.** `cfg` (classifier-free guidance) also sets the tempo: 1–1.5 gives the natural pace of the voice, 2 or more speaks faster and more pointedly. ## Training data About **8,200 hours** of studio-quality speech. The data is a private collection and is not publicly available. | Language | Hours | |---|---| | English | ~2,610 | | Polish | ~1,300 | | Spanish | ~820 | | German | ~750 | | Russian | ~645 | | French | ~500 | | Portuguese | ~300 | | Italian | ~290 | ## Training | | | |---|---| | Hardware | 1× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB) | | Schedule | 440k steps (checkpoint 430k released), 16k tokens per step, AdamW, cosine decay, bf16 | ### Compute and cost All training ran on a single rented AWS instance with **1× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB)** at **$3.36 per hour**. The figures below cover the whole rental, including setup, data processing and evaluation, not only the GPU time of the final model. Hours come from the run logs' timestamps and are approximate (±1 h per phase). #### GPU time | Phase | Period (UTC, 2026) | GPU hours | Cost (USD) | |---|---|---:|---:| | Setup: pilot runs, first OmniFish (NAR) run, audio tokenization, speaker embeddings | Oct 28 – Oct 30 | ~40 | ~$134 | | Baseline: OmniFish-BD with semantic left context (136k steps) | Oct 30 – Nov 1 | ~57 | ~$192 | | Ablations: context layouts, curricula, speaker modes, endpoint heads, MTP variants (v2–v25), axial-decoder smoke test | Nov 1 – Nov 3 | ~49 | ~$164 | | Fork A vs. fork B (axial decoder, prompt handling) | Nov 3 – Nov 4 | ~2.6 | ~$9 | | **Final model: OmniFish v26 (axial MTP decoder), 440k steps** | Nov 4 – Nov 12 | ~200 | ~$672 | | **Total** | | **~349** | **~$1,170** | The final run trains at about 2,200–2,500 steps per hour, about 100–110× real time in audio seen per hour. The ablations and the baseline account for **~$365, about one third** of the total. The final run is a little over half. #### Annotation (Gemini) Emotion and style tags and transcript checks were produced with Gemini Flash. | | Tokens | Rate (USD per 1M) | Cost (USD) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Input | 294.8M | $0.50–1.00 | ~$220–295 | | Output | 87.3M | $3.00 | ~$262 | | **Total** | **382.1M** | | **~$480–560** | Rates follow the published Gemini 3 Flash list prices. Requests went through a third-party gateway, so the amounts actually billed may differ. Another 8.9M tokens went to a fallback model and are not priced here. #### Storage Amazon S3 (us-east-2), about 1.18 TB: **~$27 per month**. Upload and same-region transfer to training machines cost nothing. #### Summary | | Cost (USD) | |---|---:| | GPU (whole rental, including ablations) | ~$1,170 | | Annotation (Gemini) | ~$480–560 | | Storage (S3) | ~$27 / month | | **Total, one-off** | **~$1,680–1,760** | The total does not include the later Audio8 fine-tune, the stage-3 experiments on a second machine, or the cost of collecting the raw data. ## Evaluation Checkpoint 430k, `cfg=1.5`, one sample per item, no cherry-picking. WER with Whisper large-v3-turbo (tags removed from the reference), speaker similarity with ECAPA2 (cosine), pitch variation as the standard deviation of F0 in semitones. **Held-out recordings** (validation set: recordings and texts never trained on, 136 items in English, Spanish and German; a voice may also appear elsewhere in training). Each item clones the voice from a 6–10 s prompt and speaks two consecutive sentences that also exist as a real recording. The real recording, passed through the same codec, is the reference. | | OGG TTS 430k | Real recording | |---|---:|---:| | WER | **1.2 %** | 2.6 % | | Speaker similarity to the prompt | **0.798** | 0.737 | | Duration vs. the real recording (median) | 0.98 | 1.00 | | Pitch variation (F0 std, semitones) | 3.90 | 4.25 | | Language | Items | WER | Similarity to prompt | Duration ratio | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | English | 54 | 1.6 % | 0.790 | 0.98 | | Spanish | 78 | 1.0 % | 0.800 | 0.98 | | German | 4 | 0.0 % | 0.885 | 0.96 | **All 8 languages** (new texts, 32 items: a neutral and an angry line per voice, voices from the training set): WER 0.5 % on average, speaker similarity 0.791. | | EN | PL | ES | DE | RU | FR | PT | IT | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | WER | 0.0 % | 1.7 % | 0.0 % | 0.0 % | 0.0 % | 0.0 % | 3.3 % | 0.0 % | | Similarity | 0.771 | 0.785 | 0.843 | 0.797 | 0.756 | 0.765 | 0.774 | 0.862 | The tempo matches real speech (duration ratio 0.98). Intonation is still about 8 % flatter than in the real recordings (pitch variation 3.90 vs. 4.25 semitones). Public benchmarks (Seed-TTS, CV3) follow. ## Limitations - Preview checkpoint: speaker similarity is not yet final, and the model may still mispronounce rare names. - Italian and Portuguese have the least training data. - Rare tags are not reliable yet. - Intonation is somewhat flatter than in real speech; `cfg` above 2 speeds the speech up. - Multi-speaker scenes in one pass are not part of this run; generate a dialogue line by line with context. ## License and responsible use - **Fish Audio codec.** The model generates Fish Audio codec tokens and needs the Fish Audio codec to produce audio. Use is subject to the [Fish Audio Community License](https://huggingface.co/FashionFlora/ogg-tts/blob/main/LICENSE-FISH-AUDIO.md) (see `NOTICE`). - **Real voices.** Do not use OGG TTS to imitate the voice of a real person without their consent, to impersonate, deceive, defraud or harass anyone, or to create sexual content involving minors. - **Research use.** The weights are released for research. ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{oggtts2026, title = {OGG TTS: Expressive Multilingual Text-to-Speech with Block Diffusion}, author = {FashionFlora}, year = {2026}, url = {https://huggingface.co/FashionFlora/ogg-tts} } ```

--- license: cc-by-nc-4.0 pipeline_tag: text-to-speech language: - en - zh datasets: - amphion/Emilia-Dataset tags: - WaveGen - wavegen - TTS - zero-shot - voice-cloning - audio - multilingual - pytorch --- # WaveGen [NeurIPS 2026] **WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning** Sang-Hoon Lee and Ha-Yeong Choi Ajou University and KT [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12527) · [Source Code](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen) · [Live Demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/LeeSangHoon/WaveGen) · [Demo Page](https://wavegen26.github.io/demo) · [Benchmark Demo](https://sh-lee-prml.github.io/wavegen-tts-demo/) · [Spectral Forcing Demo](https://wavegen26.github.io/demo/spectral_forcing_visualization/) · [WaveGen Studio (Windows)](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen-Studio) **[WaveGen Studio](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen-Studio)** runs directly on Windows without installing Python. WaveGen generates speech directly from text and reference audio using Spectral Forcing. The models are trained on English and Mandarin Chinese speech from Emilia, using **24 kHz audio** and **50 Hz waveform patches** (480 samples per patch). ## Models This repository contains the pre-trained, V-Spec, and four-step Flash checkpoints in separate folders. | Model | Checkpoint | Folder | Inference steps | |---|---|---|---| | WaveGen (Pre-trained) | 1300k EMA | `WaveGen/` | 50 | | **WaveGen (Fine-tuned with v-spec losses) — Recommended** | **1400k EMA** | **`WaveGen_VSpec/`** | **50** | | WaveGen-Flash | 48k EMA | `WaveGen_Flash/` | **4 (fixed)** | **WaveGen (Fine-tuned with v-spec losses)** is the **recommended model for inference** and the default in the source repository. All checkpoints contain **FP32 EMA weights only**, in Safetensors format. Optimizer state and other training state are excluded; these files are intended for inference, not for resuming a training run. **WaveGen-Flash** is optimized for four-step speech generation. Its complete merged weights load from one Safetensors file, together with its YAML and vocabulary. The Flash release includes inference code and model weights; its training recipe is not included. ## Seed-TTS evaluation Results on the complete standard Seed-TTS test sets for the EMA weights released here. The pre-trained and V-Spec models use **Prompt Anchor**, **Scheduled K3** (base CFG 1.25), **50 Euler steps**, Mel temperature 0, inference bottleneck dropout 0.2, and seed 0, with FP32 model weights and BF16 CUDA inference. The original test prompts are used. Flash uses **four Euler steps**, the time grid **`[0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]`**, CFG 0, inference bottleneck dropout 0, waveform temperature 1, **initial Mel temperature 0**, and seed 0. It uses the same original test prompts and FP32-weight/BF16-inference precision. Prompt states interpolate from their initial noise toward the reference at each step; the initial Mel noise is scaled by the Mel temperature. The Flash results below use the new default temperature 0. WER/CER and UTMOS are truncated to two decimal places, and SIM to three decimal places (not rounded). The complete test sets contain 1,088 English and 2,020 Chinese utterances.
Model EN ZH
WER (%) ↓ SIM ↑ UTMOS ↑ CER (%) ↓ SIM ↑ UTMOS ↑
WaveGen
Pre-trained · 1300k EMA		 1.47 0.755 3.68 1.75 0.805 2.87
WaveGen V-Spec
1400k EMA · Recommended		 1.39 0.743 3.59 1.65 0.783 2.79
WaveGen-Flash
48k EMA · 4 steps		 1.49 0.727 3.53 1.59 0.768 2.74
**WaveGen achieves state-of-the-art performance among TTS models trained on the Emilia dataset.** WER is reported for English and CER for Chinese. Error rates are percentages; all metrics are macro-averaged over utterances. The Safetensors exports preserve the FP32 EMA inference tensor values. ## Download Download the checkpoint, YAML, and vocabulary from the desired model folder and place that folder under `ckpts/` in the WaveGen source repository: ```text ckpts/ ├── WaveGen/ │ ├── model_1300000.safetensors │ ├── WaveGen_SF_Emilia_24k_50Hz_IBDrop02.yaml │ └── vocab.txt ├── WaveGen_VSpec/ │ ├── model_1400000.safetensors │ ├── WaveGen_VSpec.yaml │ └── vocab.txt └── WaveGen_Flash/ ├── model.safetensors ├── WaveGen_Flash.yaml └── vocab.txt ``` Keep each checkpoint together with its matching configuration and vocabulary. This Hub repository uses `WaveGen/`, `WaveGen_VSpec/`, and `WaveGen_Flash/` at its root; `ckpts/` is their destination in your local source checkout. ## Usage Follow the [installation instructions](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen#installation), then run from the WaveGen source repository root. Supply a reference recording, its exact transcript, and the text to synthesize. Automatic transcription is not required. ### Fine-tuned model (recommended default) ```bash python -m wavegen_v_spec.infer.infer_cli \ --ckpt_file ckpts/WaveGen_VSpec/model_1400000.safetensors \ --model_cfg ckpts/WaveGen_VSpec/WaveGen_VSpec.yaml \ --vocab_file ckpts/WaveGen_VSpec/vocab.txt \ --ref_audio reference.wav \ --ref_text "The transcript of the reference recording." \ --gen_text "The text to synthesize." ``` ### Pre-trained model ```bash python -m wavegen.infer.infer_cli \ --ckpt_file ckpts/WaveGen/model_1300000.safetensors \ --model_cfg ckpts/WaveGen/WaveGen_SF_Emilia_24k_50Hz_IBDrop02.yaml \ --vocab_file ckpts/WaveGen/vocab.txt \ --cfg_schedule scheduled_k3 \ --cfg_strength 1.25 \ --ref_audio reference.wav \ --ref_text "The transcript of the reference recording." \ --gen_text "The text to synthesize." ``` Both examples use EMA weights, **Prompt Anchor** (`Prompt_xt_Anchor`), **Scheduled K3** (base CFG 1.25), 50 steps, Mel temperature 0, and seed 0. The supplied models use inference bottleneck dropout 0.2. The pre-trained module uses constant CFG 3 when no schedule is specified, so its example selects Scheduled K3 explicitly. CUDA inference uses BF16 autocast with FP32 model weights; CPU inference uses FP32. ### Load the fine-tuned model from Hugging Face The subfolder paths below select the 1400k model from [LeeSangHoon/WaveGen](https://huggingface.co/LeeSangHoon/WaveGen). The loader resolves `main` to one commit before downloading the three assets; use a full commit SHA instead of `main` to pin a specific release. ```python import soundfile as sf import torch from wavegen_v_spec.infer.utils_infer import WaveGen torch.set_num_threads(1) model = WaveGen.from_pretrained( "LeeSangHoon/WaveGen", revision="main", checkpoint_filename="WaveGen_VSpec/model_1400000.safetensors", config_filename="WaveGen_VSpec/WaveGen_VSpec.yaml", vocab_filename="WaveGen_VSpec/vocab.txt", use_ema=True, ) sample_rate, audio = model.synthesize( "reference.wav", "The transcript of the reference recording.", "The text to synthesize.", ) sf.write("generated.wav", audio, sample_rate, subtype="PCM_16") ``` For the pre-trained model, download the `WaveGen/` folder and use the pre-trained CLI above. See the [source repository](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen) for the local Python API, Gradio demo, and batch evaluation. The source checkout defaults to the V-Spec 1400k Safetensors checkpoint. The base and V-Spec loaders support existing local `.pt` checkpoints through an explicit checkpoint-path override. ### WaveGen-Flash (4 Steps) ```bash python -m wavegen_flash.infer.infer_cli \ --checkpoint ckpts/WaveGen_Flash/model.safetensors \ --model-config ckpts/WaveGen_Flash/WaveGen_Flash.yaml \ --vocab-file ckpts/WaveGen_Flash/vocab.txt \ --ref-audio reference.wav \ --ref-text "The transcript of the reference recording." \ --gen-text "The text to synthesize." \ --output generated_flash.wav ``` Or load the same bundle directly from this repository: ```python import soundfile as sf import torch from wavegen_flash import WaveGenFlash torch.set_num_threads(1) model = WaveGenFlash.from_pretrained("LeeSangHoon/WaveGen", revision="main") sample_rate, audio = model.synthesize( "reference.wav", "The transcript of the reference recording.", "The text to synthesize.", ) sf.write("generated_flash.wav", audio, sample_rate, subtype="PCM_16") ``` The Flash loader accepts Safetensors only and requires no additional base weights. Its YAML fixes four Euler calls at `[0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5]`, ending at 1.0, with CFG 0 and IB dropout 0. The grid already includes time shift 3; it is not shifted again during inference. The final Mel output head is skipped by default; `--compute-final-mel` or `compute_final_mel=True` restores its computation. The Mel input and shared network remain active on the final call. The YAML sets `mel_temperature: 0.0` by default, while waveform temperature remains 1. Mel temperature scales only the initial Gaussian Mel noise; the clean reference Mel and later predicted Mel states are not scaled. Both noise draws are preserved even at temperature 0. Use `--mel-temperature 1` or `model.synthesize(..., mel_temperature=1.0)` to reproduce the previous initialization with the same weights. Compared with temperature 1, temperature 0 improves WER/CER, SIM, and UTMOS on both complete Seed-TTS test sets. The default duration limit is 30 seconds for prompt plus generated speech. Split longer text or explicitly increase `max_duration_seconds`; the sampler does not automatically split text. See the [Flash guide](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen/blob/main/src/wavegen_flash/README.md) for the complete inference interface. ## Safeguards and limitations - Use reference speech with the speaker's informed consent and permission to use the recording. - Do not use generated speech for deceptive impersonation, fraud, harassment, or fabricated statements presented as authentic speech. - Clearly identify shared or published outputs as AI-generated audio, and protect reference recordings and personal information. - Reference quality and transcript accuracy affect the generated speech. Pronunciation errors, omissions, repetitions, and speaker-similarity failures may occur. - For long passages, split the text into shorter segments; the single-utterance examples above do not automatically split long text. These usage guidelines are not automatic safety filters. Public-facing services should add appropriate access controls, abuse reporting, and review of suspected misuse. ## License The model checkpoints are released under [CC BY-NC 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/). WaveGen source-code contributions are released under the [MIT License](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen/blob/main/LICENSE). Reused source components retain their original licenses and notices; see the [source-code third-party notices](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen/blob/main/docs/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). ## WaveGen Studio 0.1 beta for Windows [WaveGen Studio](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen-Studio) provides a native C++ desktop interface for Windows x64, with persistent model loading, saved reference voices, text splitting, and audio editing. Python is not required to run the packaged application. This is a beta release; the original research implementation and checkpoints above remain available through [WaveGen](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen). The native model packs for Studio **0.1.0-beta.1** are stored under [`studio/v0.1.0-beta.1/`](https://huggingface.co/LeeSangHoon/WaveGen/tree/main/studio/v0.1.0-beta.1): | Pack | Contents | License scope | |---|---|---| | Flash | Exported ONNX model and frontend assets for four-step generation | WaveGen weights: CC BY-NC 4.0; retain the included source and third-party notices | | V-Spec | Exported ONNX model and frontend assets for 50-step generation | WaveGen weights: CC BY-NC 4.0; retain the included source and third-party notices | | RE-USE | Optional exported speech enhancement model derived from [NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE) | OpenMDW 1.1, with the included Apache 2.0 Mamba notice; this pack is not relicensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 | The repository's CC BY-NC 4.0 model-card label applies to the WaveGen checkpoints and their Flash/V-Spec exports. The separate RE-USE pack retains its own license and origin. Studio application code is MIT; the Windows application and runtime dependencies have their own notices and are distributed through the [Studio releases](https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen-Studio/releases). Use the Studio installer to select the model packs. It reads the versioned artifact paths, sizes, archive SHA-256 hashes, and extracted-file hashes from the root [`config.json`](https://huggingface.co/LeeSangHoon/WaveGen/resolve/main/config.json), then verifies the selected downloads against the release manifest. This file is an actual installation configuration, not a Transformers model configuration. Verified configuration and model files are reused from the local cache; no counting-only request is made. Hugging Face's download statistics are server-side request metrics and do not represent an exact count of completed installations or unique users. [`SHA256SUMS`](https://huggingface.co/LeeSangHoon/WaveGen/resolve/main/SHA256SUMS) includes the original checkpoint entries and these native archives. The native packages do not include personal reference recordings, saved user profiles, or generated speech history.

# Pocket TTS Japanese (CC BY)

Japanese models for [Pocket TTS](https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts) (Kyutai), fine-tuned
from the English 24-layer model with the official training code, **on CC BY data only**. The
weights are CC BY 4.0, so they can be used commercially, with attribution (see License). A
sibling trained with more data, under CC BY-NC 4.0, is
[takuma104/pocket-tts-ja](https://huggingface.co/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja). Code, training recipe
and the full log of results: [github.com/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja](https://github.com/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja).
How the data was built and the models were trained: technical report ([English](https://github.com/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja/blob/main/docs/report/pocket_tts_ja_report_en.pdf),
[日本語](https://github.com/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja/blob/main/docs/report/pocket_tts_ja_report_ja.pdf)).

- Runs with the **stock `pocket-tts` package** (3.3.0 or later), on CPU, with no code changes.
- Takes **plain Japanese text** (kanji and kana as written). There is no G2P front end; the model
  reads the kanji itself.
- **Zero-shot voice cloning** from a few seconds of reference audio, as in the original.

| Model | Config | FlowLM | Parameters (with the codec) | File |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| `japanese` | `japanese.yaml` | 6 layers | 110M | 219 MB |
| `japanese_24l` | `japanese_24l.yaml` | 24 layers | 336M | 1.3 GB |

日本語の概要: Kyutai の Pocket TTS を、CC BY のデータだけで日本語にファインチューニングしたモデルです。
ウェイトは CC BY 4.0 で、クレジットを表示すれば商用にも使えます（下の License を参照）。公式の
`pocket-tts`（3.3.0 以降）にそのまま読み込め、CPU で動きます。入力は漢字かな交じりの文で、読みはモデルが
決めます（G2P は使いません）。数秒の参照音声で声を指定します。Emilia（非商用）も使ったモデルは
[takuma104/pocket-tts-ja](https://huggingface.co/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja)（CC BY-NC 4.0）にあります。
学習データの作り方と学習の方法は[テクニカルレポート](https://github.com/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja/blob/main/docs/report/pocket_tts_ja_report_ja.pdf)にまとめています。

## Usage

```bash
uvx pocket-tts generate --config hf://takuma104/pocket-tts-ja-cc/japanese.yaml \
    --voice hf://takuma104/pocket-tts-ja-cc/voices/female_03.wav \
    --text "こんにちは。今日はいい天気ですね。"
```

```python
from pocket_tts import TTSModel

model = TTSModel.load_model(config="hf://takuma104/pocket-tts-ja-cc/japanese.yaml")
voice = model.get_state_for_audio_prompt("prompt.wav")
audio = model.generate_audio(voice, "こんにちは。今日はいい天気ですね。")  # 24 kHz, torch.Tensor
```

- `--voice` is a recording of the voice to clone (a few seconds of clean speech). `voices/` has ten
  synthetic voices (five female, five male, described in `voices/voices.json`), made with
  [Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small](https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small) from text
  descriptions, so they are nobody's voice. With them `japanese` reads JSUT at a Kana-CER of
  2.23% (1.3 to 3.4% per voice). Without `--voice` the CLI clones its default voice
  (alba, an English speaker), which reads Japanese as well (JSUT Kana-CER 2.00%, against 2.23%
  with the JVS prompts). The pre-made voices cannot be selected by name (`--voice alba`): they
  are embeddings computed with the official weights.
- The config sets the sampling temperature to 0.3, the value every number below was measured
  with. Classifier-free guidance (scale 2.0) is distilled into the weights.
- Use `japanese_24l.yaml` for the 24-layer model. Its config ends the audio 3 frames (240 ms)
  after the model decides that the speech is over, instead of the 5 the package would pick for
  Japanese text: the 24-layer model sometimes makes a short sound in those last frames.
- To keep a fixed version, add a commit hash: `hf://takuma104/pocket-tts-ja-cc/japanese.yaml@<commit>`.

## Results

All numbers are from generated audio transcribed by an ASR model, with speakers of the JVS corpus
(never trained on) as voice prompts, temperature 0.3, one LSD step, with the fine-tuned decoder
of the codec (see Training) unless marked.

**Kanji reading: [JKYB-Parakeet](https://github.com/Parakeet-Inc/Joyo-Kanji-Yomi-Benchmark-Parakeet-Edition)**,
all 13,536 sentences, official TTS protocol (kana-whisper). Accuracy is the share of sentences
whose target word is read correctly.

| Model | Prompts: 4 JVS speakers in rotation | Prompt: jvs001 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `japanese` | 94.77% | 94.49% |
| `japanese_24l` | 94.36% | 94.85% |
| *Original Mimi decoder:* `japanese` | 93.93% | 93.96% |
| *Original Mimi decoder:* `japanese_24l` | 93.34% | 94.08% |
| *Original Mimi decoder:* 24-layer teacher before the guidance was distilled (CFG 2.0, not released) | 92.82% | 93.82% |
| *CC BY-NC sibling* ([pocket-tts-ja](https://huggingface.co/takuma104/pocket-tts-ja), its own fine-tuned decoder): `japanese` | 94.75% | 94.84% |
| *CC BY-NC sibling:* `japanese_24l` | 94.32% | 94.49% |

**Other sets**, `japanese` with the stock package on CPU (the released bfloat16 file) next to the
GPU evaluation of the same checkpoint:

| Set | Metric | GPU | Stock package, CPU |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| JKYB-mini (1,500 sentences) | accuracy | 94.9% | 95.1% |
| Aozora Bunko ruby (1,000 sentences) | target reading accuracy | 70.7% | |
| JSUT (1,000 sentences) | Kana-CER | 2.14% | 2.23% |
| JVS zero-shot (5 male + 5 female speakers, 10 sentences each) | Kana-CER | 2.18% | 2.09% |
| JVS zero-shot | similarity to the speaker's recording of the same sentence (ECAPA) | 0.651 | 0.650 |
| Short texts (172 texts of 2–8 tokens) | did not stop / extra speech | 0 / 2 | 0 / 1 |

With the original Mimi decoder the stock package gives JKYB-mini 94.4%, JSUT 2.49% and JVS 2.15% /
0.560: the fine-tuned decoder mostly raises the similarity to the speakers' recordings (the CC BY-NC
sibling: 0.575).

`japanese_24l` (3 frames after the end of speech, as in its config) is close on these sets
(GPU: JKYB-mini 94.9%, Aozora Bunko 70.3%, JSUT 2.13%, JVS 2.47% / 0.645, short texts 0 / 0;
stock package on CPU: JKYB-mini 94.1%, JSUT 2.17%, JVS 2.30% / 0.641, short texts 0 / 0). The two
models read equally well. `japanese_24l` fails to stop and ends with a short sound a little less
often (see Limitations); `japanese` is three times smaller and faster.

## Training

1. A Japanese SentencePiece model with 4,000 pieces, trained on the transcripts of the training
   data below, replaces the English tokenizer; the text embedding is re-initialized. The codec
   (Mimi) stays frozen while the language model is trained.
2. The 24-layer teacher starts from the English 24-layer model and is trained for 580k steps
   (LSD objective, the voice prompt is another utterance of the same speaker).
3. Natural speech contains few of the rarer kanji readings, so sentences rich in them were
   synthesized with [Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small-Yomi](https://huggingface.co/takuma104/Irodori-TTS-v4.1-Small-Yomi)
   in 2,998 voices taken from Emilia-YODAS (CC BY) recordings, and kept only when an ASR model
   confirmed the reading. The words were chosen without the JKYB keys, and JKYB sentences and
   near duplicates were excluded.
4. Six frames of digital silence (the Mimi latents of silence) follow every complete training
   target and are learned like speech; the end-of-speech target stays where the speech ends. The
   stock package keeps generating for a few frames after the end of speech, and upstream training
   never shows the model those frames: without this, the model filled them with short fillers
   ("うん", "えー") after about 10% of the sentences.
5. Guidance at scale 2.0 is distilled into the weights: into a copy of the 24-layer model
   (`japanese_24l`, 50k steps) and into a 6-layer student initialized from the teacher's layers
   0, 1, 2, 21, 22 and 23 (`japanese`, 160k steps).
6. The decoder of the codec (10M parameters) is fine-tuned from the original one on CC BY audio
   only, discriminators included. First 70k steps (multi-scale mel loss, MPD and
   MS-STFT discriminators, and a loss on the batch-averaged spectrum against the tonal artifacts
   locked to the decoder's upsampling strides) on clips of up to 8 seconds: 164 hours of YODAS3
   clips cut again from the videos in full band (the training clips above whose video reaches
   15 kHz and whose DNSMOS scores are high) and 116 hours of the synthetic speech; in the last 10k of these steps the band above 4 kHz is held at the level of
   the original decoder. Then 10k steps in which the band above 4 kHz is also trained towards
   the recordings, on the YODAS3 clips with the highest predicted MOS (UTMOSv2) among those
   without band limits or clipping, female and male apart (7 to 14 hours); four such runs (three clip sets, two seeds) are averaged. Two videos
   whose voices were heard to be synthetic are left out of the decoder's data. The encoder is
   untouched, so latents and voice prompts are those of the original Mimi.

| Training data | Hours | License |
|---|---:|---|
| [YODAS3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/espnet/yodas3) Japanese, filtered, re-checked by ASR, punctuation restored | 556 | CC BY 3.0 |
| [Emilia-YODAS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/amphion/Emilia-Dataset) Japanese (the CC BY part of Emilia), filtered and re-checked by ASR | 305 | CC BY 4.0 |
| The same Emilia-YODAS clips with a changed gain | 48 | |
| Synthetic speech from Irodori-TTS (voices from Emilia-YODAS), readings confirmed by ASR | 367 | model: MIT; text: CC BY-SA, CC BY and public domain |

The synthetic texts come from Japanese Wikipedia, JMdict / KANJIDIC2 (CC BY-SA 4.0), Tatoeba (CC BY
2.0 FR), Aozora Bunko (public domain), and sentences written by LLMs for words with rare readings.
The non-commercial part of Emilia and ReazonSpeech are not used. JVS and JSUT are used for
evaluation only.

## Limitations

- About 5% of the JKYB sentences are still misread, mostly rare readings and words from the
  appendix of the Joyo kanji table (jukujikun, 86 to 88% correct). Numbers, counters and Latin letters
  were not evaluated separately.
- In 0.04 to 0.07% of the JKYB sentences `japanese` does not end the utterance and keeps
  generating up to the length limit (`japanese_24l`: 0 to 0.015%).
- 6 to 9% of the clips end with a short, quiet sound (a breath or a small voice) after a pause
  (`japanese` 8 to 9%, `japanese_24l` 6 to 7%, on JKYB-mini).
- Reading accuracy and speaker similarity depend on the voice prompt.
- Real Japanese recordings still lose clarity when they pass through the codec (Kana-CER of JVS
  recordings: 3.3% as recorded, 4.7% through Mimi with the fine-tuned decoder; 5.4% with the
  original decoder).

The prohibited uses of the original Pocket TTS apply: use of the model must comply with all

Drama 3 is a 35B text-to-speech model: it clones a voice from a few seconds of audio, plays dialogue with up to 16 speakers and follows directions such as `[sighs]` written into the text. With these files it runs on NVIDIA cards from 8 GB. > **Updated for Fish Audio's weights of 2026-10-29.** Update the nodes first, then download a model file: older nodes > refuse these files with `unexpected ['line_head.weight']`. The first release's files are in > [`v1/`](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI/tree/main/v1) and still load in the new nodes. Saved > voices keep working, and the codec is unchanged. ## Files Download one model file and the codec. All four model files hold the whole model and complete the same share of our test takes. They differ in how the routed experts, 90% of the model, are stored. | Download | Pick it for | Size | System RAM | Speed on 24 · 12 · 8 GB | |---|---|---|---|---| | [`drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors`](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI/blob/main/drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors) | Fish Audio's own expert weights, on a 24 GB card | 38.6 GB | ~48 GB | 2.7× · 1.0× · 0.6× | | [`drama3_int8experts_bf16.safetensors`](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI/blob/main/drama3_int8experts_bf16.safetensors) | The same quality on a smaller card | 38.7 GB | ~48 GB | 2.7× · 1.5× · 0.9× | | [`drama3_w6a8experts_bf16.safetensors`](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI/blob/main/drama3_w6a8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 6 GB smaller than FP8, almost as close to it as int8 | 32.7 GB | ~40 GB | 3.2× · 1.3× · 0.7× | | [`drama3_w4a8experts_bf16.safetensors`](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI/blob/main/drama3_w4a8experts_bf16.safetensors) | The fastest on any card, or 32 GB of RAM | 24.6 GB | ~32 GB | **3.8× · 2.0× · 1.0×** | | [`drama3_codec.safetensors`](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI/blob/main/drama3_codec.safetensors) | Always, with any model file | 1.6 GB | | | Speed is seconds of speech decoded per second on an RTX 4090 with the experts in system RAM, so 1.0× is real time. The 12 GB and 8 GB figures ran with the rest of the card held by another process. ## What this update changed Of 120 test takes rendered with both releases at the same seeds, 108 come out complete against 69, and the takes that went silent fell from 48 to 1. The int8, W6A8 and W4A8 files are now tuned on the model's own speech, so W4A8, the fastest file, completes as many takes as FP8. ## Samples Rendered with these weights. The cloned voices come from two public-domain films of 1948 and 1954 with uncredited narrators, and from open speech corpora recorded for research by anonymous volunteers; the other voices are invented by the model. Each take names its source. [More on the demo page](https://pedromarinhodev.github.io/ComfyUI-Drama3/#listen), with the script lighting up as it plays. **News from the workshop**: a cloned voice announces this update > [1940s newsreel announcer, brisk and triumphant] News from the workshop! The talking machine has learned new tricks. > It speaks faster, [pause] it forgets fewer lines, [chuckles] and it no longer falls silent in the middle of a > sentence. [lowering his voice, confidential] Engineers say the secret is practice. [triumphant] Lots and lots of practice! Voice: the uncredited narrator of [Our Food and Our Health](https://archive.org/details/gov.dod.dimoc.29761) (1948), a US Department of Defense film in the public domain. **Nine Garys**: two cloned voices in one dialogue > <|speaker:0|> [upbeat podcast host] Welcome back to Plant Talk! Today my co-host is going to introduce us to his houseplants.
> <|speaker:1|> [completely deadpan] This is Gary.
> <|speaker:0|> [warmly] Hi, Gary! And the one by the window?
> <|speaker:1|> [deadpan] Also Gary.
> <|speaker:0|> [suspicious] How many plants do you have?
> <|speaker:1|> [deadpan] Nine. They are all Gary.
> <|speaker:0|> [laughing] Doesn't that get confusing?
> <|speaker:1|> [slightly offended] Not for the Garys. Voices: anonymous speakers p294 and p237 of the [CSTR VCTK Corpus](https://datashare.ed.ac.uk/handle/10283/3443) (CSTR, University of Edinburgh, 2019), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), each used as a voice reference for this take. **The hunt**: a cloned voice, whispered > [hushed nature documentary narrator, barely above a whisper] Here, in the long grass of the living room carpet, the > house cat waits. Her prey: a single grey sock, alone and unaware. [whispers] She has stalked it for eleven minutes. > [tense] The tail twitches. The haunches rise. [excited whisper] And she pounces! [pause] [disappointed] She has > missed. [dry] She will now pretend this never happened. Voice: the uncredited narrator of [Surprise for Jean](https://archive.org/details/SurpriseForJ) (1954, Encyclopaedia Britannica Films), public domain.
More: four invented voices, Brazilian Portuguese **The heist**: six lines, four voices the model casts itself > <|speaker:0|> [gravelly heist leader, whispering] Alright. The vault opens in sixty seconds. Roles?
> <|speaker:1|> [far too cheerful] I'm the distraction!
> <|speaker:2|> [nervous, talking fast] I'm the hacker. I've hacked... a vending machine before.
> <|speaker:3|> [elderly woman, perfectly calm] I'm only here to collect my pension, dear.
> <|speaker:0|> [long pause] [sighs] Who invited the pensioner?
> <|speaker:1|> [proudly] She's my grandma. She's the getaway driver. Voices: invented by the model. **A confissão**: a cloned Brazilian voice > [galã de novela, dramático, voz trêmula] Helena, eu preciso te contar uma coisa. Aquele bolo de chocolate que sumiu > da geladeira... [soluça] fui eu. [desesperado] Eu comi tudo! [pausa] [baixinho] E comeria de novo. Voice: an anonymous Brazilian Portuguese speaker of [Google FLEURS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/fleurs) (Google, 2022, pt_br, utterance 1574), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), used as a voice reference for this take.
## Quick start **1. Install the nodes.** Search for **Drama 3 text to speech** in ComfyUI-Manager, or clone [ComfyUI-Drama3](https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3) into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes`, and restart ComfyUI. Nothing to `pip install`. **2. Download** a model file, the codec and, for the transcripts of voice clips, Qwen3-ASR. From the `ComfyUI` folder: ```bash hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors --local-dir models/diffusion_models hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI drama3_codec.safetensors --local-dir models/vae hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI qwen3_asr_1.7b_bf16.safetensors --local-dir models/asr ``` **3. Open the workflow** `example_workflows/drama3_voice_clone.json` from the nodes, pick a few seconds of clean speech, write your text and run. For dialogue, start each line with `<|speaker:N|>` and give each speaker a voice. You need ComfyUI v0.40 or newer and system RAM of the model file plus about 8 GB. Script syntax, dialogue modes and troubleshooting are in the [nodes' README](https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3#readme).
How these files were made From [fishaudio/drama-3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3) at its revision of 2026-10-29: - **FP8**: the routed experts' FP8 bytes and 128×128 block scales copied unchanged, gate and up projections fused (the nodes' `tools/convert.py`). - **int8, W6A8, W4A8**: the experts dequantized from FP8 in fp32 and quantized again in ComfyUI's comfy_kitchen layouts: int8 ConvRot (per-channel int8 after a rotation in groups of 256), or 6-bit or 4-bit weights. Each expert's rounding is then tuned with GPTQ in the rotated basis, on 66,000 rows of the model's own takes weighted by how much each expert was used, which cuts the experts' output error by 60% (gate and up) and 31–33% (down) against plain rounding on held-out rows. The layouts are the stock ones: ComfyUI's loader reads them as they are. - **Every file**: the attention, DeltaNet, shared-expert and codebook-decoder layers are the checkpoint's own bf16; the LM head keeps only the rows generation samples from. - **Codec**: Fish Audio's S2-Pro codec as shipped with Drama 3, weight norm folded in, fp32; byte-identical between the two releases of the weights. Distance from the FP8 file with its expert routing forced, over 2,391 held-out audio frames; the first row is the FP8 file through plain float matmuls. A take is *complete* when Qwen3-ASR hears at least three quarters of its words, no silent tail was cut and the frame cap was not reached. | File | Hidden state | KL, nats | Top token | Complete takes of 120 | |---|---|---|---|---| | FP8 (the floor) | 1.12% | 0.0025 | 96.5% | 108 | | int8, tuned | 1.22% | 0.0026 | 96.5% | 109 | | W6A8, tuned | 1.60% | 0.0033 | 95.9% | 108 | | W4A8, tuned | 4.10% | 0.0066 | 93.2% | 108 |

# Voce di Jarvis: Qwen3-TTS 1.7B in GGUF e ONNX

*English summary at the bottom of the page.*

Questo archivio contiene la voce di **Jarvis**, un assistente vocale per Windows con scheda video NVIDIA: il modello
[Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base) (sintesi vocale con clonazione del timbro da un
breve riferimento audio) già **convertito** per girare in locale con llama.cpp (talker e predictor, GGUF) e ONNX Runtime
(decoder ed encoder). Non è un modello nuovo e non è stato riaddestrato: sono i pesi ufficiali di Qwen, convertiti e
quantizzati. L'installer di Jarvis lo scarica da qui, file per file, e controlla l'impronta SHA-256 di ciascuno.

Non è un prodotto commerciale: è un pacchetto per un progetto personale (l'assistente Jarvis), senza garanzie, e non ha
alcun legame con Qwen o con Alibaba Cloud.

## Modificato

**Modificato rispetto all'originale: convertito in GGUF e ONNX.** Nessun addestramento e nessun fine-tuning.

- il talker è scritto in GGUF e quantizzato Q5_K, il predictor in GGUF e quantizzato Q8_0 (`llama-quantize` di llama.cpp, build b10621);
- il decoder audio e i due encoder (codec e timbro) sono esportati in ONNX e portati a FP16 (LayerNorm, Softmax e Range restano in FP32);
- le tabelle degli embedding sono estratte in file NumPy e il tokenizer del testo è riscritto in un solo `tokenizer.json`.

## Provenienza

| Parte | Origine |
|---|---|
| Modello | [`Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base), revisione `fd4b254389122332181a7c3db7f27e918eec64e3` (Apache 2.0) |
| Codec audio | [`Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-Tokenizer-12Hz`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-Tokenizer-12Hz), revisione `7dd38ad4e9bad454aae9cd937d0cd577604fe229` (Apache 2.0) |
| Conversione | [HaujetZhao/Qwen3-TTS-GGUF](https://github.com/HaujetZhao/Qwen3-TTS-GGUF), commit `74feb581bc8cefb835fc608107e857036d7580a1` (licenza MIT), con i suoi script di esportazione usati senza modifiche |
| Quantizzazione GGUF | `llama-quantize` di [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp), build b10621 |

## I file

Tutti i percorsi sono relativi alla radice dell'archivio, che ha la stessa forma della cartella `voce\qwen-gguf\modello` di
Jarvis. Totale: 2.445.006.206 byte (circa 2,45 GB, 2,28 GiB).

| File | Che cos'è | Formato | Byte |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `embeddings/codec_embedding_0.npy … codec_embedding_15.npy` | 16 tabelle di embedding dei codici audio, una per livello del codec | NumPy FP32 | 276.826.112 |
| `embeddings/proj_bias.npy` | bias della proiezione per il predictor | NumPy FP32 | 4.224 |
| `embeddings/proj_weight.npy` | matrice di proiezione 2048 → 1024 per il predictor | NumPy FP32 | 8.388.736 |
| `embeddings/text_embedding_projected.npy` | tabella degli embedding del testo (151.936 × 2048), già proiettata | NumPy FP16 | 622.329.984 |
| `qwen3_tts_codec_encoder.fp16.onnx` | encoder del codec: trasforma la voce di riferimento in codici | ONNX FP16 | 114.173.449 |
| `qwen3_tts_decoder.fp16.onnx` | decoder audio: dai codici alla voce a 24 kHz | ONNX FP16 | 230.028.143 |
| `qwen3_tts_predictor.q8_0.gguf` | predictor: completa i 16 livelli del codec (142 milioni di parametri) | GGUF Q8_0 | 151.124.320 |
| `qwen3_tts_speaker_encoder.fp16.onnx` | encoder del timbro della voce di riferimento | ONNX FP16 | 24.462.132 |
| `qwen3_tts_talker.q5_k.gguf` | talker: il modello di linguaggio (1,42 miliardi di parametri) che genera i codici audio | GGUF Q5_K | 1.006.245.120 |
| `tokenizer.json` | tokenizer del testo, in un solo file | JSON | 11.423.986 |

Gli embedding del testo sono in FP16; le tabelle dei codici audio e la proiezione sono in FP32.

## Come si usa

- **Con l'installer di Jarvis** (il modo normale): l'installer scarica i file nella cartella `voce\qwen-gguf\modello` del
  programma, con gli indirizzi fissati a una revisione precisa (`https://huggingface.co/Aikonex/jarvis-voce/resolve/<commit>/<file>`)
  e l'impronta SHA-256 di ogni file nel suo manifesto: se qualcuno cambiasse i file di questo archivio, l'installer li
  rifiuterebbe, perché l'impronta non corrisponderebbe.
- **A mano:** serve il motore [HaujetZhao/Qwen3-TTS-GGUF](https://github.com/HaujetZhao/Qwen3-TTS-GGUF) al commit
  `74feb581`: `TTSEngine(model_dir=<questa cartella>, onnx_provider="CUDA")`, con Python 3.14, ONNX Runtime 1.31.1 per CUDA
  (CUDA 13 e cuDNN 9 dai pacchetti NVIDIA) e i DLL di llama.cpp b10621 per CUDA 13.3.
- **Requisiti:** scheda NVIDIA con CUDA. Misurato sulla RTX 4070 Ti: circa 2,1 GB di memoria video, avvio in 4-5 s, primo audio
  in circa 190 ms, voce più di 4 volte più veloce del parlato.
- Il modello Base clona il timbro da una voce di riferimento di pochi secondi, insieme alla sua trascrizione esatta
  (`--rif voce.wav --testo-rif voce.txt`). Le voci che propone l'installer di Jarvis sono sintetiche, create con
  [Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign) da una descrizione a parole: non
  appartengono a nessuna persona reale. Clonare la voce di una persona reale richiede il suo consenso esplicito.

I file di questo archivio sono derivati dai pesi di Qwen3-TTS (Qwen Team, Alibaba Cloud) e sono distribuiti con la stessa
licenza, **Apache 2.0**: il testo è nel file `LICENSE`. Gli archivi Qwen3-TTS su Hugging Face non includono quel file; la copia qui

cioè lo stesso testo Apache 2.0 (l'anno nell'appendice è quello del file originale). Il motore di conversione e di inferenza è di
HaujetZhao (MIT) e non è incluso.
