This repository is a ready-made voice pack for **Jarvis**, a local Windows voice assistant (NVIDIA GPU required). It contains
[Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base) (revision `fd4b254389122332181a7c3db7f27e918eec64e3`)

# VoxMel

**VoxMel** is a tokenizer-free continuous autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) framework that directly models mel-spectrograms through a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform. A language-model backbone with a flow-matching head generates **Coarse-Mel** autoregressively; two non-autoregressive residual tiers recover temporal and frequency details without feeding them back into the autoregressive history. A separate Vocos vocoder converts the reconstructed mel-spectrogram into speech.

[![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-VoxMel-blue?logo=github)](https://github.com/VoxDance-Lab/VoxMel)
[![Demo-page](https://img.shields.io/badge/Web-Demo-orange)](https://voxdance.github.io/voxmel-demo/)


## Highlights

- **Direct mel modeling** — No learned acoustic tokenizer or compressed acoustic latent space; the text frontend uses the Qwen2.5 tokenizer.
- **Exactly invertible decomposition** — Frequency and temporal Haar splits preserve all mel coefficients. Exact invertibility applies to the transform, rather than guaranteeing lossless generated audio or vocoder reconstruction.
- **Coarse-only autoregression** — Generate Coarse-Mel first, then the temporal residual and frequency residual in dependency order. Residual details stay outside the autoregressive history.
- **English and Chinese zero-shot cloning** — Synthesize speech from reference audio and its transcript, with 24 kHz output in the paper's configuration.
- **Post-training** — Frozen-head GRPO improves all four Seed-TTS metrics.




## Quick Start


### Installation

Use Python 3.10–3.12. Install matching PyTorch and torchaudio builds for your
hardware (the original environment uses torch/torchaudio 2.4.1 with CUDA 12.1),
then install from the repository root:

```bash
pip install -e .
```

`requirements.txt` is shared by the package installer. Vocos is included.
For CPU or Apple Silicon, use the appropriate PyTorch build. `device="auto"`
selects CUDA, then MPS, then CPU; an unavailable explicit device raises an error.
MPS operator support and performance still require validation with your checkpoint.

### Prepare Model Files

This checkout includes model code and a Qwen tokenizer, but **no trained VoxMel
weights, experiment config, or Vocos weights**. Supply a compatible experiment:

```text
/path/to/experiment/
├── config.yaml
└── model_L_final.pt
/path/to/vocos-mel-24khz/
├── config.yaml
└── pytorch_model.bin
```


### Python API

```python
from voxcore import VoxMel
import soundfile as sf

model = VoxMel.from_pretrained(
    "/path/to/experiment",
    tokenizer_path="examples/voxmel/qwen_tokenizer",
    vocos_path="/path/to/vocos-mel-24khz",
    device="auto",
)

# Audio continuation cloning requires the exact reference transcript.
wav = model.generate(
    "这是声音克隆的演示。",
    prompt_wav_path="reference.wav",
    prompt_text="参考音频中实际说出的内容。",
    cfg_text_strength=3.5,
    cfg_spk_strength=3.0,
    seed=42,
)
sf.write("clone.wav", wav, model.sample_rate)
```

The API returns a mono float32 NumPy waveform and runs in inference mode. `min_seconds` and `max_seconds` control coarse-frame generation bounds; model stop predictions affect actual duration. `cfg_text_strength` and `cfg_spk_strength` independently control text and speaker guidance, while `up_num_steps` sets residual solver steps. Speaker guidance applies only when reference audio is provided.

# Eka (एक) · audio8-nepali

Eka is Ampixa's Nepali fine-tune of [Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.1b](https://huggingface.co/Audio8/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.1b).
Give it a few seconds of someone speaking and some Nepali text, and it reads the text in that voice.
The release checkpoint is **eka-ft-v7**. Release page: [ampixa.com/eka](https://ampixa.com/eka/).

**Small, natural-sounding, and Nepali rather than Hindi-accented.** Eka's generator has just **170M parameters**, half of Swar's
337M and a quarter of OmniVoice's 613M, and it runs on a laptop CPU. On NepTTS-Bench (205 sentences) it has the highest UTMOS (4.07)
and SCOREQ (4.50) of every model we tested, and on our [Hindi Leak Scorer](https://ampixa.com/blog/does-a-nepali-tts-voice-still-say-it-the-hindi-way/)
it is flagged about half as often as Swar or OmniVoice:

| Model | Generator parameters | UTMOS ↑ | SCOREQ ↑ | Hindi leak flags ↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Eka (eka-ft-v7)** | **170M** | **4.07** | **4.50** | 18 / 103 |
| Eka (eka-ft-v9) | 170M | 4.02 | 4.48 | **15 / 103** |
| OmniVoice | 613M | 4.02 | 4.17 | 34 / 104 |
| VoxCPM2 | 2.31B | 3.91 | 4.07 | 55 / 91 |
| Swar | 337M | 3.88 | 4.36 | 36 / 100 |
| Stock Audio8 (our starting point) | 170M | 3.67 | 4.22 | not run |

**Against stock Audio8**, the same 170M model before our training: character error on NepTTS-Bench fell from **92.0% to 13.8%**
(Naamche cloning bench: 84.5% to 8.8%), UTMOS rose from 3.67 to 4.07 and SCOREQ from 4.22 to 4.50. Same size, same speed; only the weights changed.

UTMOS and SCOREQ are automatic naturalness predictors (higher is better). Hindi leak flags count readings where key words
moved toward Hindi pronunciation (lower is better).

## Try it on a CPU in two minutes

No GPU, no PyTorch, no account needed. `onnx/` is eka-ft-v7 and `onnx-v9/` is eka-ft-v9, both ONNX INT8 for CPUs.

```bash
pip install "onnxruntime==1.23.2" "numpy<2.5" soundfile scipy tokenizers huggingface_hub
hf download ampixa/audio8-nepali --include "onnx/*" --include "onnx-v9/*" --include "runtime/*" \
    --include "voices/*" --include "examples/*" --local-dir eka      # about 1.6 GB (each model alone: about 820 MB)
cd eka

# Built-in voice (OpenSLR 43 speaker 0546)
python examples/speak.py --text "नमस्ते, म एक हुँ। म नेपाली बोल्छु।" --out hello.wav               # eka-ft-v7
python examples/speak.py --model v9 --text "नमस्ते, म एक हुँ। म नेपाली बोल्छु।" --out hello_v9.wav  # eka-ft-v9

# Your own voice: 4 to 10 seconds of one person speaking, and exactly what they say in it
python examples/speak.py --model v9 --ref me.wav --ref-text "मेरो नाम राम हो, म काठमाडौँमा बस्छु।" \
                         --text "आज बेलुका खाना खान घर आउँछु।" --out me.wav
```

Want only one model? Download `onnx/*` for v7 or `onnx-v9/*` for v9 (about 820 MB each; the codec files are the same).
Each `--include` takes one pattern.

It prints how long the audio is and how long it took. On an Apple M3 Pro with 4 threads we measured RTF 1.18 on a
39-second paragraph (a little slower than real time); short sentences take longer per second of audio because the
voice prompt is processed first. v7 and v9 run at the same speed. If a sentence comes out empty or runs on, try another `--seed`.

**Known problem:** on an Intel i5-10400 (AVX2, no VNNI) the INT8 build produced broken audio for most test sentences,
while the same files and settings were fine on Apple Silicon. Test on your own CPU before relying on it on older Intel
machines; we are working on a fix.

### Streaming (experimental)

`--stream` hands out audio in chunks while it is still generating, and reports when the first audio arrived and how
often a listener would have heard a pause. `--play` does the same and plays it through your speakers
(`pip install sounddevice`). The finished file is the same as without streaming.

```bash
python examples/speak.py --text "नमस्ते, म एक हुँ। म नेपाली बोल्छु।" --play
python examples/speak.py --text "नमस्ते, म एक हुँ। म नेपाली बोल्छु।" --stream --chunk-frames 24 --out s.wav
```

On a laptop CPU it is not smooth yet. To keep the joins exact, every chunk re-decodes about 6 seconds of earlier audio,
and that decoding is the slow part. Apple M3 Pro, 4 threads, default 48-frame chunks (about 2.2 s each):

| Text | First audio | Pauses | Done (streaming) | Done (normal) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sentence, 5.5 s of audio | 4.5 s | 2, totalling 2.5 s | 11.4 s | 7.7 s |
| Paragraph, 13.9 s of audio | 4.9 s | 6, totalling 16.4 s | 34.6 s | 16.3 s |

Smaller chunks start sooner but pause more (12 frames: first audio at 2.8 s, 9 pauses on the sentence). To make a file,
leave streaming off.

## v7 or v9?

Both run the same way; pick with `--model`.

- **eka-ft-v9: fewer word and pronunciation errors.** Choose it when the words matter most: reading text aloud,
  announcements, anything where a wrong word is worse than a slightly different voice.
- **eka-ft-v7: closer voice match.** Choose it when sounding like the reference speaker matters most. It is the
  checkpoint the release film and benchmarks headline.

If unsure, render the same sentence with both and listen. On 20 public NepTTS-Bench sentences with the built-in voice
and the same seed, the CPU builds scored 12.5% (v7) and 10.2% (v9) character error by the MMS recognizer; v9 was better
on 10 sentences, worse on 6, tied on 4.

## Which checkpoint to use

All nine fine-tunes are here under release names. The root `model.safetensors` is eka-ft-v7.

| Release | File | What it is | sha256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| eka-ft-v1 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v1/` | Wave 1 supervised (318.8 h), step 6000 | `327bca23…` |
| eka-ft-v2 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v2/` | Wave 2 supervised (575 h), step 3000 | `dcaa61f9…` |
| eka-ft-v3 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v3/` | Wave 2 supervised, step 6000 | `4452b7c8…` |
| eka-ft-v4 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v4/` | Wave 3 supervised, final | `73e1c134…` |
| eka-ft-v5 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v5/` | Wave 4 supervised, step 2000 | `30512a90…` |
| eka-ft-v6 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v6/` | Preference training (DPO), round 1 | `eb0f19e5…` |
| **eka-ft-v7** | `model.safetensors`, `checkpoints/eka-ft-v7/`, `onnx/` | **DPO round 2. The release.** | `a555f6c0…` |
| eka-ft-v8 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v8/` | DPO round 3, step 129 | `0ab717ef…` |
| eka-ft-v9 | `checkpoints/eka-ft-v9/`, `onnx-v9/` | DPO round 3, step 258. Fewest word errors | `451ef4a9…` |

- **On a CPU:** eka-ft-v7 (`onnx/`) and eka-ft-v9 (`onnx-v9/`).
- **Most accurate words:** eka-ft-v9, on every independent recognizer we used, at a small cost in voice match.
- The others are PyTorch only (load them with this repo's `modeling_arktts.py`; a GPU is recommended).

| | eka-ft-v7 | eka-ft-v8 | eka-ft-v9 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Character error, 23 voices not in training (MMS) | 16.3% | 15.1% | **12.6%** |
| Character error, Naamche cloning bench clean | 8.8% | 8.7% | **7.5%** |
| Voice match, Naamche cloning bench (ECAPA) | **0.52** | 0.51 | 0.48 |
| Hindi Leak Scorer flags | 18 / 103 | not run | **15 / 103** |

No significance test has been run between these three.

## How it compares

Naamche cloning bench v1.1, clean track, 64 prompt and sentence pairs (our harness reproduces Swar's published numbers):

| System | Character error | Voice match | UTMOS |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Eka (eka-ft-v7)** | 8.8% | 0.52 | 3.24 |
| Swar | 5.6% | 0.69 | 2.67 |
| OmniVoice | 5.0% | 0.70 | 2.63 |
| VoxCPM2 | 9.0% | 0.68 | 2.40 |
| Audio8 base | 84.5% | 0.34 | 2.73 |

[Hindi Leak Scorer](https://ampixa.com/blog/does-a-nepali-tts-voice-still-say-it-the-hindi-way/) v84 (frozen), same
26 sentences in 4 voices: IndicF5 60/93, VoxCPM2 55/91, Swar 36/100, OmniVoice 34/104, **Eka v7 18/103**, Eka v9 15/103.
A flag is a candidate for a listener, not a confirmed error.

Generator size: Eka 170M parameters (plus a 130M codec decoder), Swar 337M, OmniVoice 613M, VoxCPM2 2.31B.

All of these are automatic scores; there is no listening panel yet. Training exposure of the bench voices is unknown
for every system, so the tables are not rankings. Eka's weakest point is voice match.

## Files

- `model.safetensors`, `config.json`, `modeling_arktts*.py`, `processing_arktts.py`, tokenizer files, `codec.pth`:
  the PyTorch model (root weights = eka-ft-v7; until 2026-11-11 the root was eka-ft-v1).
- `checkpoints/eka-ft-v1` … `eka-ft-v9`: every fine-tune, by release name.
- `onnx/`: eka-ft-v7 ONNX INT8 (same files as [ampixa/audio8-nepali-dpo-onnx](https://huggingface.co/ampixa/audio8-nepali-dpo-onnx)
  @75800398). `onnx/registration/` is the codec encoder used to register new voices.
- `onnx-v9/`: eka-ft-v9 ONNX INT8, made with the same weight-swap method onto Audio8's INT8 graphs
  ([Edge0/audio8-TTS-0.1B-ONNX-INT8](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/audio8-TTS-0.1B-ONNX-INT8)); that method reproduces the
  `onnx/` v7 build byte for byte. Codec, encoder and tokenizer files are identical to `onnx/`.
- `runtime/arktts_runtime_0_1b/`: the ONNX runtime from [Audio8-AI/Audio8_TTS](https://github.com/Audio8-AI/Audio8_TTS)
  @4eb54a69, unmodified, Apache-2.0.
- `voices/slr43-0546/`: a sample voice from OpenSLR 43 (Google, ne_np_female), CC BY-SA 4.0.
- `examples/speak.py`: the test script above, including `--stream` and `--play`.

## Licence and use

Weights: [Audio8 Community License v1.0](https://huggingface.co/Audio8/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.1b). It bars commercial use at
or above US$2M annual revenue and requires consent before cloning a real person's voice. Clone only voices you have
permission to use, and disclose synthetic speech where required. The runtime is Apache-2.0; the sample voice is
CC BY-SA 4.0 (attribution: OpenSLR 43, Google).
